articles.title: CedarDB wants one database to handle both transactions and analytics, as AI agents raise the stakes | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Databases have traditionally been designed either for analytical data or for operational data. But database engine CedarDB supports both, and its approach has gained relevance with the rise of agentic AI.
articles.body:
Databases have traditionally been built for one of two jobs. Analytical databases help businesses spot trends and answer questions, while operational databases store the day-to-day records of transactions, like orders and payments. But the Munich-based database engine CedarDB supports both, and its approach has gained relevance with the rise of agentic AI, its co-founder and CEO Moritz Sichert told TechCrunch.

CedarDB has been in the making for the last decade, but its current momentum stems from enterprise companies whose existing data stacks may have been well suited to storing years of transactions, yet less suited to quickly answering analytical questions asked in natural language about that data.

CedarDB’s questioning of the divide between analytical and operational queries is a by-product of its focus on efficiency. The company is a Technical University of Munich spinout based on Umbra , a research project that was built from scratch to beat legacy database engines at processing speed by making the most of modern hardware.

With five Umbra researchers as its co-founders, CedarDB kept that approach, promising faster performance without requiring more CPUs or processing power and memory — and requiring few changes from customers. In particular, its team made sure CedarDB was compatible with PostgreSQL , an open source database system.

According to Sichert, this compatibility with the popular database helps keep switching costs low, since users don’t need to rebuild their apps. It also has an added advantage: CedarDB follows the logic LLMs are most familiar with as a result of their training.

That decision is one of many choices that proved lucky in retrospect, Sichert said. But it wasn’t all luck. In a blog post , co-founder Christian Winter detailed key priorities the team set after leaving academia, “such as reliability, fault tolerance and compatibility with popular tools.”

Not all of the answers were obvious. The team strongly debated whether it should launch a cloud offering right away. In the end, it launched CedarDB Enterprise as an on-premise offering alongside its free version, CedarDB Community Edition, both announced in May of last year at the same time as it announced a €5.3 million seed funding round (approximately $6 million).

The cloud offering was only delayed, though, not abandoned. After conducting beta testing with users who had signed up for its waitlist, the company on Wednesday announced limited availability of CedarDB Cloud onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt , where it’s competing with 20 other startups vying to win TechCrunch’s prestigious Startup Battlefield competition.

A fully managed, cloud-hosted version will likely help CedarDB expand its user base beyond large enterprises. It will also make it better prepared to compete with the likes of Databricks, a major data company that seems to have reached the same conclusion as the German startup.

At its Data + AI Summit in June, the American company cited “the agentic era” as the reason why it was launching LTAP , a new data architecture aiming to “[unify] transactions, analytics, streaming, and operational data on a single copy of storage in the lake.”

It is too early to tell how disruptive this might be, but Sichert interprets Databricks’ move as another sign that there is demand for what CedarDB does. The startup plans to serve its first cloud users with its current team of 14 people, but Sichert expects it will need a larger team once it gets more traction. “And this is where we would raise our next round.”

Pictured from left to right: CedarDB founders Moritz Sichert, Lukas Vogel, Philipp Fent, Dominik Durner, and Christian Winter.

articles.title: Intero Biosystems wants drugmakers to test on mini human intestines, not animals | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Intero Biosystems is selling lab-grown human intestines to drugmakers as regulators push for alternatives to animal testing, while the startup looks to scale production and expand its organoid technology.
articles.body:
Drug development has long relied on animal models, but differences between species mean what works in animals doesn’t always translate to humans, and most drugs still fail during development. Intero Biosystems , a Denver-based startup, is developing human intestinal organoids, lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, as another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. Researchers and pharmaceutical companies are increasingly looking for models that better reflect human biology to supplement animal testing and reduce their reliance on it.

Intero, which spun out of the University of Michigan, says its organoids differ from simpler models that replicate only part of the gut. They contain multiple cell and tissue types found in the human intestine, which the company believes makes them a more human-relevant model for testing drugs and other compounds, co-founder and CTO Madeline Eiken told TechCrunch.

“Most drugs fail clinical trials, and I think it’s pretty easy to appreciate that we are neither mice nor flat layers of cells,” Eiken said.

The startup’s flagship product, GastroScreen , is a human intestinal organoid model that it sells to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds. Each organoid is about one millimeter across, and the company ships roughly 100 at a time in a tube, co-founder and CEO Charlie Childs said. Customers can use them as healthy intestinal models or induce disease-like conditions to test how the tissue responds to different compounds.

“We’re literally shipping mini living organs in the mail to people,” Childs said.

Beyond the organoids themselves, Intero sells the supplies needed to grow and work with them, such as the nutrient mixes that feed the cells and the chemicals used in experiments. It also runs studies for customers, including designing custom experiments, performing lab tests, and delivering the resulting data. Much of this work focuses on drug safety and disease research. For example, a customer can expose the organoids to a drug candidate to see whether it could harm the gut, or use organoids modeling a gut condition to see how the tissue responds to a compound.

Founded in 2024, the startup now has seven employees and just under 10 customers after raising a $2.3 million pre-seed round last year. It generated more than $400,000 in revenue from the fourth quarter of last year through the third quarter of this year, the CEO noted.

Regulatory changes have also helped drive interest in alternatives to animal testing. In April of last year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) laid out plans to reduce its reliance on animal testing in drug development, promoting alternatives including organoids, organs-on-chips (small devices that mimic organ functions) and AI-based computational models as potential alternatives.

In March of this year, the FDA issued draft guidance outlining how drug developers should validate new approach methodologies, or NAMs, a term of non-animal testing methods, when using them to support regulatory submissions. The guidance provides a framework for validation but doesn’t endorse any specific method. Whether a NAM can support a submission depends on factors including the method, how it is used, and the data provided.

Changes in U.S. law that allow drug developers to use non-animal testing methods in some cases have made pharmaceutical companies more willing to explore technologies such as organoids, Eiken told TechCrunch. Companies once hesitant about the technology are now looking to bring organoids in-house, she added.

Intero isn’t alone in trying to build more human-relevant models of the gut. Altis Biosystems develops stem cell-derived intestinal models, while InSphero offers patient-derived intestinal organoids for gastrointestinal toxicity testing. Other peers like MIMETAS take a different approach with organ-on-chip technology, using microfluidic systems to recreate aspects of the environment inside human tissues.

Intero says it sets itself apart from competitors in the complexity and scalability of its model. Unlike intestinal models grown from tissue collected through procedures such as colonoscopies, GastroScreen is derived from induced pluripotent stem cells, which are adult cells reprogrammed to become almost any cell type and can be generated from a blood sample, Eiken explained. That approach gives the startup the potential to personalize its models to different patients and scale production more easily, she added.

When asked what evidence shows GastroScreen can predict human drug responses more accurately than existing animal or cell-based models, Childs said the company is still building that evidence and is now in the second stage of a three-stage validation process. Having first shown that GastroScreen contains the key tissues of the human gut, Intero is now testing well-known drugs with documented effects in humans. GastroScreen has shown expected responses to drugs that reduce intestinal inflammation and to compounds known to damage the gut, Childs told TechCrunch. In the final stage, the company will compare GastroScreen’s results directly with pharmaceutical companies’ existing animal and clinical data. Those studies are underway with several pharmaceutical companies, using both existing compounds and new drug candidates, Childs said.

Intero doesn’t use AI to build its organoids. Instead, Childs sees an opportunity to use the organoids to generate the biological data AI models need, and the company plans to license such datasets to pharmaceutical and AI companies.

In the near term, Intero is focused on scaling production. It can currently make a few thousand organoids at a time and is working to automate manufacturing, with the goal of producing hundreds of thousands per batch, Childs said. Longer term, it wants to move into personalized medicine, using a patient’s cells to create organoids that could test different drugs before treatment. Its most ambitious goal is an artificial intestine, a vision that Childs said would build on the manufacturing scale and patient-specific data generated through its organoid technology.

Intero took the stage earlier Wednesday at TechCrunch Disrupt, where it’s one of 20 startups vying for this year’s Startup Battlefield title. Join us for the rest of the action: Disrupt runs October 13 to 15 in downtown San Francisco.

articles.title: Gudea leverages AI to help organizations prevent social media crises before they erupt | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Every day, conversations unfold across social media and websites around the world. A seemingly insignificant post—whether it involves AI-generated
articles.body:
Every day, conversations unfold across social media and websites around the world. A seemingly insignificant post—whether it involves AI-generated misinformation, hate speech, or a damaging rumor—can quickly snowball into a much larger public controversy.

Gudea , a company that tracks how stories and rumors spread online that describes itself as the “storm tracker for the internet,” is using AI to help organizations spot trouble brewing online before it turns into a crisis.

Unlike traditional social listening platforms, which only track metrics such as mentions, hashtags, and impressions, Gudea aims to show organizations who is driving a conversation, how information is moving, how quickly a story is gaining traction, and where it could be headed. Rather than simply tallying posts, its AI analyzes behavior, relationships, and the pathways through which information travels across more than 500 mainstream and fringe websites and platforms, including X, Reddit, and TikTok.

Instead of simply telling a company that mentions are rising, Gudea aims to provide the context behind that growth so decision-makers can determine how and whether to respond.

Gudea pitched its mission Wednesday afternoon on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , where the company made the case that companies need to take a more proactive approach to protecting their reputations.

“These big industries don’t understand that there are things they can do proactively to defend their reputation and their brand,” CEO and founder Keith Presley said. “A lot of the chief communications officers and chief media or marketing officers, they’re using legacy tools to try to figure out what’s happening. Those tools were only ever designed to tell you the number of hashtags or number of impressions.”

Gudea was founded in 2023 by Presley, Jonathan Sperber, and James Thomin. Presley brings more than 15 years of experience spanning political campaigns and defense, including building the infrastructure for Andrew Yang’s presidential campaign. Sperber, the company’s chief strategy officer, has a background in disinformation research. Thomin, Gudea’s CTO, holds a Ph.D. in chemical engineering and has spent roughly two decades working in AI and machine learning.

Presley called the company’s path to becoming a startup unusual.

“We’re one of those weird startups where I never wanted to do a company,” he said.

The team began with the George Washington Initiative, a nonprofit established after the 2020 election. The organization adapted strategies and tactics that the intelligence community has used overseas to disrupt online networks tied to groups such as Al Qaeda and ISIS. It applied them to domestic information campaigns.

The goal was to identify the online environments where information campaigns were taking shape and disrupt the pathways that allowed those narratives to reach wider audiences.

However, the team found that existing tools didn’t show how information was actually moving across people, groups and platforms. That gap became the opening for Gudea.

Three years after its founding, Gudea has nearly 40 clients. According to Presley, its customer base includes a Fortune 50 telecommunications company, a Fortune 50 retailer, “one of the world’s largest AI labs, one of the world’s largest bands,” public relations and crisis communications agencies, and government agencies.

With the rise of generative AI, Presley believes that the need for Gudea’s technology has only grown, as the company looks to expand its customer base.

AI tools have dramatically lowered the cost and effort required to generate content and coordinate online campaigns. What once required a larger organization can increasingly be carried out by a single person with a laptop and access to the right software.

“When we first started in 2021, and then as a company in 2023, we maybe saw one out of four things we looked at have inauthentic activity around it,” Presley said. “Now it’s probably nine out of ten things that we look at have this inauthentic activity.”

Looking further ahead, Gudea plans to expand its ability to understand where narratives originate and how they spread. One major upcoming initiative is geolocation for narratives. Slated for next year, the technology is intended to allow users to identify where conversations are happening with far greater precision, down to the city-block level, Presley explains.

The company also wants to give customers greater access to the tools behind its analysis. For example, a company could eventually run an advertising campaign through Gudea’s AI model before launching it and get a better idea of whether the strategy is likely to produce a negative outcome or not.

Last week, Gudea announced that it had raised $7 million in seed funding in a round co-led by Mudita Venture Partners and Silicon Road Ventures. The investment brings the startup’s total funding to approximately $15 million.

articles.title: Professora Maria do Carmo defende câmeras em fardas de policiais | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidata do PL ao governo do Amazonas é a primeira a participar da série de sabatinas do JAM2, que segue nesta sexta-feira (16).
articles.summary: Maria do Carmo (PL) iniciou as sabatinas do JAM2 com propostas para segurança, saúde e combate a queimadas no Amazonas. Confira os detalhes da entrevista.
articles.body:
A candidata ao governo do Amazonas, Professora Maria do Carmo (PL), afirmou que pretende ampliar o efetivo do Corpo de Bombeiros e das polícias ambientais, além de implantar câmeras corporais para policiais. As propostas foram apresentadas durante entrevista ao Jornal do Amazonas 2ª edição (JAM 2), da Rede Amazônica, nesta quinta-feira (15).

Ao falar sobre segurança pública e prevenção de incêndios, a candidata disse que o estado precisa recompor o efetivo das forças de segurança, melhorar os equipamentos e se preparar para eventos climáticos recorrentes, como queimadas, secas e enchentes.

“Nós temos que ampliar o efetivo das polícias ambientais, do Corpo de Bombeiros, preparar os brigadistas, formá-los permanentemente”, afirmou.

A candidata foi a primeira a participar da série de sabatinas do JAM2, que segue nesta sexta-feira (16) com o candidato Omar Aziz (PSD).

Veja o que Professora Maria do Carmo falou sobre os seguintes temas:

Prevenção de queimadas e eventos climáticos

Durante a entrevista, Professora Maria do Carmo afirmou que o Amazonas precisa se preparar para eventos climáticos recorrentes, como queimadas, secas e enchentes. Segundo ela, a falta de planejamento faz com que o estado enfrente dificuldades para responder a essas situações.

A candidata citou a necessidade de ampliar o número de brigadistas, investir em ações preventivas nas comunidades e preparar equipes para combater incêndios.

“Nós temos que nos preparar para esses eventos já prevendo o que vai acontecer. Se acontecer, estaremos preparados. E, se não acontecer, as coisas continuam como estão”, declarou.

Questionada sobre a elaboração de um plano de adaptação às mudanças climáticas, ela disse que pretende preparar a logística do estado para reduzir o isolamento de moradores do interior durante os períodos de seca.

Entre as medidas citadas estão a recuperação de estradas que ligam municípios e o planejamento para garantir o deslocamento de moradores quando a navegação pelos rios for prejudicada.

Reforço no efetivo do Corpo de Bombeiros

Maria do Carmo também afirmou que pretende ampliar o efetivo das forças de segurança, realizar concursos públicos e melhorar os equipamentos utilizados pelos profissionais.

Ao falar sobre o Corpo de Bombeiros, ela declarou que o efetivo está defasado em mais de 1.500 profissionais. A candidata também criticou a estrutura disponível no interior do Amazonas e disse que pretende investir na construção e melhoria de unidades.

“Nós temos que retomar, fazer concursos públicos, para retomar o Corpo de Bombeiros e reaparelhar”, afirmou.

Ela também defendeu a formação permanente de brigadistas e o aproveitamento das guardas municipais do interior, onde houver, para preparar equipes para responder a incidentes climáticos.

A candidata também foi questionada sobre o uso de câmeras corporais por policiais, em meio a dados apresentados durante a entrevista sobre prisões de agentes de segurança no Amazonas.

Maria do Carmo disse ser favorável à medida e afirmou que os equipamentos podem oferecer proteção tanto às vítimas quanto aos próprios policiais.

“Acho que isso é preciso. É uma garantia não só para vítimas, para as polícias também, para os policiais”, declarou.

Ela também afirmou que pretende adotar práticas utilizadas em outros estados, recompor o efetivo policial por meio de convocações e novos concursos e melhorar os equipamentos de trabalho dos agentes.

A candidata citou ainda a necessidade de fornecer uniformes aos policiais, para que os profissionais não precisem comprar as próprias fardas.

Atendimento a mulheres vítimas de violência

Questionada sobre violência contra a mulher, Maria do Carmo defendeu o aumento do número de delegacias especializadas e a ampliação da Ronda Maria da Penha, voltada à proteção de mulheres em situação de violência doméstica.

Durante a entrevista, o assunto foi abordado após uma pergunta sobre uma decisão da Justiça Eleitoral envolvendo dois apoiadores da candidata, em um caso relacionado a supostas ameaças contra Alessandra Campêlo , candidata a vice-governadora na chapa de Omar Aziz.

Maria do Carmo afirmou que considera necessário rigor na atuação das autoridades e disse que pretende ampliar a estrutura de atendimento às mulheres.

“Nós temos que ser rigorosos”, declarou.

A candidata também afirmou que pretende construir a Casa da Mulher Brasileira no estado e ampliar as casas de acolhimento. Segundo ela, a estrutura existente da Casa da Mulher Brasileira ainda precisa ser concluída.

“Não, ela vai ter que ser construída, porque ela não existe hoje. Ela só tem aí uma carcaça”, disse.

Maria do Carmo também defendeu que mulheres de diferentes classes sociais tenham acesso ao mesmo nível de proteção e atendimento nas delegacias e nos órgãos do sistema de Justiça.

Maria do Carmo afirmou que pretende realizar mutirões em parceria com a rede privada para reduzir as filas por consultas, exames e cirurgias eletivas no Amazonas. Segundo ela, a meta é começar a estabilizar as demandas mais urgentes nos primeiros 100 dias de governo.

A candidata também defendeu o pagamento das dívidas da saúde e a regularização dos serviços prestados nos hospitais estaduais. Ela criticou as condições das unidades, citando falta de reformas e equipamentos.

“Resolver a situação da saúde é prioridade máxima”, afirmou.

Para acelerar os atendimentos, Maria do Carmo propôs parcerias com hospitais e laboratórios privados, inclusive para utilizar o período noturno na realização de exames.

Maria do Carmo afirmou que pretende defender a Zona Franca de Manaus e melhorar o modelo econômico. Questionada sobre o posicionamento de Flávio Bolsonaro, seu aliado político, em relação à Zona Franca, ela disse que ele mudou de opinião após conhecer o polo industrial do estado.

A candidata declarou que o modelo é indispensável para a economia amazonense e defendeu a atração de novas indústrias.

“Não tem como dispensar esse modelo, que, aliás, eu acho que o Brasil inteiro deve ao Amazonas essa floresta em pé, a nossa Zona Franca”, declarou.

Questionada sobre como se posicionaria caso Flávio Bolsonaro fosse eleito presidente e defendesse alguma medida prejudicial ao modelo, Maria do Carmo afirmou que seria contrária à proposta.

“Certamente contrário a ele, porque nós temos que defender com unhas e dentes esse modelo”, disse.

A candidata também propôs criar um escritório permanente em Brasília, com técnicos para acompanhar medidas de interesse da Zona Franca.

A candidata defendeu a criação de novas atividades econômicas para reduzir a dependência do Amazonas em relação à Zona Franca de Manaus.

Entre as áreas citadas estão a mineração legalizada, a exploração de gás natural, a produção de fertilizantes, o setor primário e o turismo.

“Eu quero investir fortemente na infraestrutura, na criação de novas matrizes econômicas, no setor primário”, afirmou.

Maria do Carmo também defendeu investimentos em ensino técnico de acordo com as necessidades do mercado de trabalho. Segundo ela, a proposta é preparar jovens para ocupar vagas no Polo Industrial de Manaus.

A candidata citou ainda o fortalecimento das escolas agrícolas e a formação de profissionais para desenvolver atividades econômicas no interior do estado.

Na área de infraestrutura, Maria do Carmo afirmou que pretende concluir, no primeiro ano de governo, a estrada que liga Anori a Codajás.

“A gente vai realmente focar que, no primeiro ano do nosso governo, a gente vai finalizar essa estrada”, declarou.

Ela também defendeu investimentos em outras rodovias e a retomada de obras paralisadas no interior do Amazonas.

Ao falar sobre as prioridades dos primeiros 100 dias de gestão, a candidata propôs uma força-tarefa para enfrentar problemas de infraestrutura em estradas, escolas e hospitais.

Maria do Carmo também citou a proposta de construir uma Via Expressa Oeste, que, segundo ela, ligaria a região da Ponta Negra à área das Aparecidas. A candidata afirmou que pretende tentar viabilizar o projeto nos dois primeiros anos de governo.

“A gente está diante de eleições que hoje estão polarizadas. De um lado, temos Lula e Omar; do outro, Maria do Carmo e Flávio Bolsonaro, por um Brasil que precisa avançar. Estamos com o Brasil caótico e o Amazonas também está perdido. O Amazonas precisa avançar, o interior precisa avançar, e nós estamos com essa proposta. Pense bem, você que mora no interior: sua vida, por todos esses últimos anos, a saúde está boa? A educação está boa? A infraestrutura está boa? Não adianta nada a gente ter prefeitos que não ajudam. A gente precisa ter um governo que trabalhe, que invista e que valorize o povo do interior, porque o Amazonas só vai ser forte se tivermos o interior forte. Ainda temos tempo. Eu sempre digo que a gente está reclamando do tempo, mas é isso. Gente, no próximo dia 25, você sabe qual escolha fazer. Muito obrigada.”

articles.title: Meet the five companies competing in the Startup Battlefield finals at Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
articles.summary: It’s time to unveil the five companies that will be competing in the Startup Battlefield finals.
articles.body:
Over the past two days, 20 startups have been pitching on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , presenting live demos and answering tough questions from our expert judges. Now it’s time to unveil the five companies that will be competing in the Startup Battlefield finals.

This year’s Battlefield spanned four categories — space and physical AI, energy and manufacturing, health tech and life sciences, and enterprise and security — and our finalists are working on everything from miniature human organs to fighting scams to computing in space.

The finals will kick off tomorrow (Thursday) at 11:30 am Pacific — you can watch them on stage at Disrupt or on the livestream here. The founders will be presenting for another panel of expert judges who will pick the winner; that winner gets to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000, equity-free.

Apate deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, with different ages, genders, and accents, speaking various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.

Flox Intelligence has built a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently than the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away. Instead, it uses edge devices with perception systems trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away.

Intero Biosystems is developing human intestinal organoids — lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, as another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. Its organoids differ from simpler models that replicate only part of the gut. They contain multiple cell and tissue types found in the human intestine, which the company believes makes them a more human-relevant model for testing drugs and other compounds.

Industrial Next builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context, and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks, without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor. In fact, some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones.

Satlyt is building software designed to allow many satellites to share the work of large computing jobs in space. The startup has already flown its software on two demonstration missions, with an initial focus on finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft. Those spacecraft typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise, with communication, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings. The next goal: to show that it can create a shared computing cloud between two satellites.

articles.title: Figma announces new features to define how agents work on its platform | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Figma is also releasing its code layers feature in open beta.
articles.body:
Design platform Figma announced a new Markdown-based editor to help define a company’s design, bring in design and code libraries, and integrate with the Payload headless content management system during the company’s first Config event in India. Through some of these features, the company aims to provide a definition for its own and third-party agents to adhere to a brand’s design rules better while creating with AI.

The company debuted a new feature called Figma Specs, which is a markdown editor that lets users define their design language in a simple way. The document can serve as a reference for teams and agents while designing in Figma. Specs can exist as a standalone file in Figma or can co-exist within the canvas. Apart from acting as a text editor, users can reference other Figma elements, such as elements on the canvas and embed FigJam diagrams, code layers, and designs.

What’s more, teams can bring in more context about design, including design libraries, code libraries, and guidelines to manage context for the design system. Agents can also refer to this centralized system to adhere to rules.

In the past week, the company made its agent on canvas available to a wider user base. However, given the non-deterministic nature of AI, the company is providing tools to steer it towards more predictable outcomes.

Figma also made its code layers feature, which adds coding to designs on canvas for more interactive prototypes. The company announced this feature in private beta back in June. At its India event this week, the company is making the function available in public beta to let more users test it out. Users can also ask the agent to turn a design into code or change a part of the code to iterate on a prototype.

“We see Figma as the place where software teams come to decide what they build and ship. And so for that, I think one of the key things to keep in mind about what AI has changed and what it made available is the ability to build,” Figma’s chief design officer Loredana Crisan told TechCrunch. “There are 17-times more lines of code being produced today than in the past. But when you’re looking at releases, only 1.3-times more releases. A lot of that code actually is not necessarily built to ship, but really built to discover what the product is. It’s built to design.”

The company said it is also supporting over 20 new tools with its MCP, including Open Code, Dia, Grok Bot, and Indian AI startup Sarvam.

Last year, Figma acquired open-source headless CMS Payload . Now, the company is integrating it with its Figma Make product for generating dynamic websites and directly managing content. The company said that Payload’s downloads have increased sixfold in the last 12 months.

The company opened its first office in India late last year with sales , partnership, go-to-market, and product support functions. Figma said that the country is its biggest market in terms of users outside the United States. The company noted that the platform works with 40% of India’s top 100 companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange.

articles.title: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani invests $29.2 million into New York University's quantum lab; says: We are building a city where economic justice doesn't come at the...
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has committed $29.2 million in city money to New York University's (NYU) new quantum technology lab, and the city wants
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has committed $29.2 million in city money to New York University's (NYU) new quantum technology lab, and the city wants a share of whatever comes out of it. Under a deal announced on October 14, New York City will receive 15% of NYU's central administration proceeds from any intellectual property created at the lab using tools the city helped fund. It also gets three seats on the lab's executive advisory board.The Quantum Fabrication Facility, or QFab, will occupy 23,000 square feet at 770 Broadway in Manhattan and is expected to open in 2030. NYU is adding $255 million of its own, $100 million for construction and $155 million for a decade of operations, which takes the project to $284 million. "We are building a city where economic justice doesn't come at the expense of innovation," Mamdani said.New York City will get a 15% cut of NYU quantum lab proceedsThe city's share covers equity, royalties, milestone payments and patent licences. If a startup built on QFab research goes public or gets acquired, part of that payout comes back to the city. Mamdani called the agreement a new national standard, then added, "or, as we say in the industry, a standard model."Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su said that when the public invests in a technology at the start, it should share in the success. She has also said the 15% figure isn't a magic number, and that it's too early to estimate what the deal could earn.That uncertainty is the main criticism. Aaron Bartnick, a Columbia University fellow and former Biden White House official, has argued that venture capitalists would treat an early-stage quantum bet as high risk, and questioned whether taxpayers signed up for that kind of exposure.Asked at the event whether President Donald Trump, whose administration has taken stakes in private companies, inspired the model, Mamdani replied: "No, he's not the inspiration."QFab opens quantum chip-making tools to CUNY students and startupsThe lab will house cleanrooms, cryogenic systems and a deep-ultraviolet lithography stepper. NYU Tandon Executive Dean Juan de Pablo said startups can't afford such a machine on their own but need it for prototyping. It can print around 300 million transistors on an 8-inch silicon wafer, each roughly 1,000 times smaller than the width of a human hair.Students from the City University of New York (CUNY), starting with Borough of Manhattan Community College and City Tech, will train there too. De Pablo put that number at over 3,000 and said he wants to extend access across the CUNY system. Public school students get summer bootcamps. Over its first decade, QFab is expected to support more than 100 companies and reach 35,000 New Yorkers, while NYU plans to add 35 faculty and postdoctoral positions.New York City bets on a $2.7 trillion quantum industryQuantum technology is projected to generate up to $2.7 trillion in global economic value by 2035. De Pablo said the number of quantum startups in the city has quadrupled to more than 80 in six years, many working alongside IBM. What they lacked, he said, was a facility like this one.Mamdani opened the event by running through New York's scientific firsts, from the discovery of deuterium at Columbia in 1931 to DNA research at the Rockefeller Institute. He then added a 15-year-old in the Bronx who scored 91 on his biology Regents exam in 2007. "In case you're wondering, he's now the mayor," he said.The payoff from QFab, if it comes, is still years out. The lab opens in 2030, and turning its chips into products will take longer. What the city has secured for now is a written claim on that future, and a say in what gets built.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ramp reaches $60B valuation as it pushes deeper into AI
articles.summary: The funding comes as Ramp's annualized revenue crosses $2B, and its customer count reaches 85,000.
articles.body:
Expense management company Ramp said on Thursday that it had raised $1.85 billion in a new funding round that values it at $60 billion, just four months after raising $750 million at a $44 billion valuation .

The financing was co-led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Sands Capital, and Avenir Growth.

Ramp said its annualized revenue has crossed $2 billion, up from a reported $1.5 billion in June, and that its revenue growth is 25% faster than it was around this time last year. The company claims it now facilitates annualized purchase volume of over $275 billion, up 175% from a year earlier. It also says it has 85,000 customers, up from 70,000 in June, including Visa, Uber, Shopify, Robinhood, Anduril, Notion, Cursor, and Figma.

The funding comes as Ramp has been expanding beyond expense management into payments, fraud detection, procurement, vendor management, and, of late, even accounting.

The startup has also built an AI story around itself, embedding AI agents into its procurement, expense management, accounting, budgeting, and other products. It also launched a corporate credit card specifically designed for AI agents to use, and in August entered the model routing business to tap the booming AI inference market and give existing clients a model routing service that fits neatly with its current products, including AI token usage monitoring and token spend management.

Earlier this month, Ramp launched Glass , a workspace that collects and remembers the AI automations, prompts, and skills that an organization’s employees build so others can take advantage of the company’s collective knowledge and skills.

“In just a few years, Ramp has become a much broader financial operations platform, with AI deeply embedded in how the company builds and operates. We believe Ramp is well on its way to becoming one of the defining companies of this era,” Christian Jensen, partner at Dragoneer, said in a statement.

Other investors in the round include Capital International, Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, D1 Capital Partners, Greenoaks, ICONIQ, GIC, 8VC, 1789 Capital, Alpha Wave Global, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Coatue, D.E. Shaw, Definition Capital, FirstMark, General Catalyst, Generation Investment Management, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Pinegrove Opportunity Partners, Soma Capital, and Stripes.

The company has now raised about $5 billion in funding.

As Ramp has widened its product lineup, it has increasingly run into Rippling, the HR and payroll software company that has pushed into corporate cards, expense management, and bill payments. The overlap puts the two companies in direct competition for the same finance-team budgets.

Early investor Keith Rabois, who has backed Ramp through two firms, Founders Fund and Khosla Ventures, both of which participated in this round, spoke to TechCrunch last month about Ramp’s strategy and his own big ambitions for the company.

“Ramp is not worried about Rippling,” Rabois said. “We’re going to compete with Anthropic,” he continued. “That’s the goal. I want to be larger and more successful and more important than Anthropic. Ramp is going to be the primary way people manage their token spend, how they optimize it, how they measure ROI, and that will lead us to collide probably with Anthropic in many ways.”

With additional reporting from Connie Loizos

articles.title: SK Hynix bargains for chip equipment exports to its China facility in return for building a factory in US | TechCrunch
articles.summary: SK Hynix’s Solidigm is reportedly seeking U.S. approval to send more chipmaking equipment to China as it weighs building a new NAND chip factory in America.
articles.body:
SK Hynix appears to be navigating choppy U.S.-China chipmaking waters. The company’s flash memory unit, Solidigm, is seeking U.S. approval to send American chipmaking equipment to its factory in Dalian, China, as a condition to continue building a semiconductor factory in the U.S., Reuters reported , citing anonymous sources.

Solidigm has been reportedly chalking up plans to build a NAND flash memory chip factory in the U.S. and is considering upstate New York as a potential location for the facility.

NAND flash chips are primarily used in solid-state storage drives, which are employed in everything from laptops and smartphones to AI data centers. But the global component shortage, thanks to skyrocketing demand for AI data centers, has driven up prices for everything that goes into data centers, including high-speed RAM chips and SSDs. Research firm TrendForce expects NAND prices to rise 15% to 20% in the fourth quarter.

Reuters cited its sources as saying that Solidigm wants to install more chipmaking equipment in spare space at SK Hynix’s Dalian factory in China to boost NAND chip production.

SK Hynix told TechCrunch it is not seeking to expand capacity at its Dalian Mod B facility, which was completed in 2023. The chip giant added that the equipment installation is being carried out in consultation with and under authorization from the U.S. government.

Washington first imposed sweeping restrictions on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment exports to China in October 2022, citing national security concerns, and further tightened the rules in 2023 . Then in September 2025, the Trump administration revoked special export exemptions for certain SK Hynix, Samsung, and Intel facilities in China. The U.S. has since granted an annual license to Samsung and SK Hynix for sending chipmaking equipment to their plants in China.

The U.S. has also been pushing foreign chipmakers to build and expand their manufacturing facilities in America. In July, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said he wanted Samsung and SK Hynix to build chip plants in the country and that he was in talks with both companies.

Solidigm is said to be preparing for a 2027 U.S. IPO that could raise around $10 billion and value it at up to $100 billion.

articles.title: Volvo makes a bigger bet on Nvidia for hands-free automated driving | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia that will extend beyond its battery electric vehicles.
articles.body:
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways.

Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.

The Alpamayo stack is redundant and diverse, according to Ali Kani, who heads up Nvidia’s automotive division. It combines Alpamayo, a family of AI models, datasets, and simulation and development tools used to build autonomous-driving software, with classical software that uses machine learning and camera and radar perception, he said.

“The point is we run these two stacks at the same time, and we have multimodal sensors in our philosophy because it’s a safer product that way,” Kani said, adding that the open source Alpamayo software has now been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers.

Volvo didn’t reveal the value of the partnership or which vehicle model would be the first to use this new Nvidia tech stack. But Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo’s head of software development, hinted at the scale of the deal and how it represents the automaker’s evolution toward developing a full-tech stack designed for its electric vehicles as well as its plug-in hybrids and gas-powered vehicles.

“Automakers used to be very much like car-line-based development and working with various suppliers, etc. and we have completely changed and migrated into being a full-tech stack company,” Bakkenes said, adding that Volvo will start this partnership with a brand new vehicle that “will come in the not-too-near future.”

He said the first vehicle with this new Nvidia tech stack will debut within the decade, and “then of course the technology can go beyond that.”

While Volvo’s relationship with Nvidia isn’t new, the expanded partnership represents the automaker’s effort to bring the latest automated driving software to all of its vehicles — not just its EVs.

All of Volvo’s battery-electric vehicles use Nvidia’s Orin computer chip, which processes information from cameras, radar, and other sensors to help a vehicle understand its surroundings and make driving decisions.

“What we’re going to do in the future is actually standardize more on Hyperion — also from a sensor set perspective — to really open up the stack for the wider partnership with Nvidia,” Bakkenes said.

articles.title: Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Bluesky is bringing “social vibe coding” to its experimental Attie platform, allowing users to create interactive experiences like games, quizzes, and websites that can tap into the social network's audience.
articles.body:
Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences.

The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform , which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build.

These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere.

Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”

The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era.

Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this.

“Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.”

When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles.

To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang.

“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”

That network today has 47 million registered users , though it’s seen a decline in engagement , as some users who tested it out later returned to X.

Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said.

“There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.”

articles.title: Bluesky wants to make it easier to buy, sell, and fundraise on the network | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only path to monetization, and that there are alternative models that are feasible when it comes to monetization.
articles.body:
Bluesky plans to introduce payments in the coming months, a first step in its strategy to make money without relying on advertising. CEO Toni Schneider and COO Rose Wang outlined the plans Thursday at TechCrunch Disrupt , explaining how the company hopes to build on the commerce and fundraising activity already happening on its decentralized social network.

“People are actually selling things, fundraising very successfully, supporting each other on the network,” Schneider said. “We want to make that easier, and the way we’re going to do this is if you see something on the network that you like and support, you can support that monetarily, and we want to do it in a way that works for Bluesky and for all the other apps out there as well, so that it works across the entire network.”

Schneider, the former CEO of Automattic, took the reins of the company in March after longtime CEO Jay Graber stepped down. He said, while onstage, that he was surprised by the reaction to his appointment, with some users joking that it marked the beginning of the end for the platform. Those comments reflected fears that a leadership change would bring unwanted changes to Bluesky.

Schneider said he understands that users can leave Bluesky for another platform if the company introduces features or changes they dislike, a reality that he said keeps the leadership team accountable as it prepares to introduce monetization in the coming months.

The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only viable business model for a social network.

“I think there’s a story around monetization that feels like advertising is the inevitable thing we have to do that will ruin the network,” Wang said. “What was really promising about having Toni join us is he built at WordPress Automatic a $10 billion business where a billion of it goes back to the parent company and the rest of it goes to the ecosystem.”

Wang also pointed to Bluesky’s status as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which she said puts the company’s mission at the center of its business strategy.

“Yes, we need to make money, but because of our infrastructure, we cannot lock people in,” Wang said. “And so the thing that really matters for us is the people who are creating value on the networks these days are the ones who are getting the value that is coming in or the money that’s coming in. And I kind of think of it as like feudal society where we’re working for a few landlords and they dictate everything, and then we have to pay up our dues as tariffs.”

Bluesky aims to give users ownership of their digital identities and control over their networks while creating a more open internet where value and revenue can flow directly to the people who generate them.

“First, we’ll start with payments, but I think it’s about disrupting the actual infrastructure layer, which is what we’re doing, and not just building another app,” Wang said.

articles.title: And the winner of Startup Battlefield at Disrupt 2026 is: Intero Biosystems | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Intero Biosystems beat out 199 other Startup Battlefield companies to take home the $100,000 grand prize at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.
articles.body:
For three days this week in San Francisco, 20 eager startups participated in the Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 . The top 20 were chosen to represent the best of the Startup Battlefield 200 , and they competed for a chance to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000. With that intense pitching now complete, we have a winner.

These startups all presented a live demo in front of the VCs and tech leaders who judged the competition.

After hours of deliberations, TechCrunch editors pored over the judges’ notes and narrowed the list down to five finalists: Apate, Flox Intelligence, Intero Biosystems, Industrial Next, and Satlyt.

The final five made their way to the finale to demo in front of our final panel of judges: Alexa von Tobel of Inspired Capital, Chi-Hua Chien of Goodwater Capital, Dayna Grayson of Construct Capital, Karl Alomar of M13, and Stacy Brown-Philpot of Cherryrock Capital.

We’re now ready to announce that the winner of TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 2026 is:

Intero Biosystems is a Denver-based startup founded by Charlie Childs and Madeline Eiken that spun out of the University of Michigan. It’s developing 1 mm human intestinal “organoids,” lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, offering another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. The startup sells its flagship product, GastroScreen, to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds.

Apate is an Australian startup founded by Dali Kaafar, who came up with the idea while doing research at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia. It deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims, answering scam calls, responding to shady messages and emails, following phishing links, and joining social media groups to bait fraudsters. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more.

These two companies now join the ranks of Startup Battlefield winners and finalists like Trello, Discord, Cloudflare, and Mint on the Disrupt Stage. articles.title: When it came to Cal AI's viral success, a small army of influencers paid off | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.
articles.body:
Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.

Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.

Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.

“From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.”

The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”

Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.

Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much.

“I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter.

Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million .

Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app.

articles.title: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The new car used thrusters to leap over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 at a demo in Texas.
articles.body:
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”

Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion.

“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”

Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph accleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.

All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour.

Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”

Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.

Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket.

Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.

“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year . Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.

“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”

Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.”

The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns , which was on display at the event.

In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.

“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote.

Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.

Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”

But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later , at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.

“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.

These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

“They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028,” Brownlee posted Thursday. “This is a prank, right?”

articles.title: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Benchmark says the Valley’s rule against backing rivals is getting harder to keep.
articles.body:
For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule.

It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies.

Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10-to-15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference.

“The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.”

Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.”

Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.”

He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said.

Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added.

Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid.

articles.title: Replit's CEO says the future of work is the 'self-driving company' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Replit CEO Amjad Masad envisions a future of “self-driving companies,” where AI agents handle day-to-day tasks and people focus on higher-level decisions.
articles.body:
Replit CEO and co-founder, Amjad Masad , has seen how AI is impacting the workplace first-hand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them.

He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgement and taste.

“The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.

He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year.

“Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.”

Illustrating the shift, the Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed.

And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent.

“You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained.

The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on.

“We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.”

He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said).

“There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.
